en: Influencing the Assembly:
A Poem on the Pure Land of the Bodhisattva Bhikṣuṇī Samudrareṇuśrī.

Able to manifest from the Realm of Endurance in the Western Quarter, whenever a person’s faith and aspiration are strong, the World-Honored One of Compassion constantly receives and guides them there;
immediately, he manifests the wondrous fragrance of the lotus.
The face of Mount Lu and the ancestral style of the old house: the direct heir has personally transmitted the Way, which is inherently the same.
Since attaining Buddhahood ten kalpas ago, Amitābha is perfectly united within my own mind.
The Pure Land is clearly manifest before one's eyes; there is no need to take a step to question the Golden Immortal. Who will be the first to find the path to the Land of Bliss?
One’s own home mountain lies but a few inches away at the edge of the setting sun.
Ruins and brambles are the true Pure Land; seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are the ancient Amitābha.
If one can simply forget all discrimination in the present moment, clap one's hands and laugh "he-he" while chanting "li-lo."

Upholding the precepts adorns the body; the retribution of merit is true. Upon ground of golden sand, there is the springtime of jade towers. Simply contemplate the Amitābha Buddha of one's own nature;
throughout kalpas, how could it ever be stained by a single speck of dust?
One must form the karmic connection for the Pure Land of the West; let all notions of self and other be completely cast aside. With every step, one is in the Lotus Land;
once the shore is reached, what need is there to seek a boat again?
The Buddha’s words and the mind of dhyāna do not differ in the least. Peach blossoms red and plum blossoms white—both are but flowers.
Upon the ground of lapis lazuli, golden grains are strewn; before the steps of agate, jade sands are spread.
Sitting alone in a secluded dwelling, ten thousand anxieties are forgotten; the entire body is entirely the King of Dharma. Cease using delusion and enlightenment to obstruct the eye of the mind;
the flowers of perfect awakening bloom, their fragrance pervading the world.

Occasionally acting in a dazed and carefree manner is indeed folly; yet, being clearly and thoroughly penetrating, there is truly no knowing. All purposeful activity and movement are fundamentally not consciousness;
it is like water and moon intersecting, reflecting in a green pond.
The six sense-bases dissolve into a single point of stillness; the evening sun sets in the west as the moon circles in the east. This ready-made koan need not be raised;
lie high upon the northern window with the door left unfastened.

Twenty-four Poems on Contemplating the Seasons (Selection of Three) At the Start of Insect Awakening, hearing thunder, all things revive. Do not seek within this the signs of flourishing or decay. The mountain stream before me flows from a living source;
Thoroughly clear and pure, it remains unstained by filth.
On the spring equinox, the orioles sing along the purple roads. A single fleecy cloud accompanies me in my dwelling. The bright moon and pure breeze cannot detain me;
carefree and at ease, I let them drift east or west.
The great snow falls in profusion like clusters of silk floss; high mountains and level plains are viewed as one.
In every head and every object lies infinite meaning—how many practitioners of Zen are deceived by their own eyes!
Untitled: Behold this solitary man; he is truly a guest of nothingness. Moving in and out, coming and going, he wanders at ease without leaning on a staff.
Having no affection for children, nor any pressure from wife or children, he happens to sit beneath a tree and beholds the white blossoms of the plum.
I travel until the end of the mountains, where I sit and watch the clouds arise. White clouds fly across the horizon; the red sun remains suspended in the sky.

The vast blue sea turns to mulberry fields; hills and mounds are leveled until no ground remains. Arising and ceasing are like bubbles on the water; gathering and dispersing are but the play of children.
How lamentable are those who have become monks: they have not heard the sound of the Buddha's teaching; they know only to gorge themselves on food, failing to awaken to their original nature.
All day long, mind and objects contend, as they are entangled in profit and fame. How long can such a state endure? In an instant, one becomes but a heap of dust.
This morning marks the first day of the year; the New Year is an auspicious day. [Dong-gu] Dong-gu—the drums and gongs resound. Every person is adorned in ceremonial robes and headdresses.
When meeting, all bow respectfully; during tea conversations, they joyfully perform the *yī* salutation. Everyone celebrates the New Year, yet I say it is but the old days.
A guest of the cold crags in the stone chamber, unaware of day or night, I have forgotten the passage of years and months as I sit. Too lazy to transform sentient beings.
Truly a man who has realized for himself; he fears neither thieves, tigers, dragons, nor snakes. When asked about the price of rice in Luling, what would he say now?
He speaks only of the emptiness of the world, yet at all times he acts within the realm of existence. Emptiness does not empty itself, nor does existence exist of its own accord.

Emptiness and existence have been non-existent from the beginning; since there is nothing to be had, why must one guard against nothingness? When discussing the dust of the world, the wild jackal howls; when speaking of the Truth, the lion roars.
Guests passing through from ancient times to the present are busy rushing about day and night; for what reason do they crave honor, and for what purpose do they scheme for profit as merchants?
Wealth and nobility bring but momentary joy, while the hells endure for ten thousand kalpas. The journey ahead is long and far; why not return home early?

A human lifespan does not exceed a hundred years, yet those who die young are even more pitiable. How much more so when one encounters the perils of the world’s path, where every step forward only leads further away.
Affection and love must inevitably end; the karmic ties between enemies and kin remain unresolved. In the Land of Ultimate Bliss beyond birth and death, liberation is naturally secure.
Yet karma remains unpurified and never dries up; sentient beings cling to every place. Turn your head and reflect inwardly: all that revolves around you is but a temporary sojourn.
Simply realize that the fundamental nature is empty; all conditions naturally fall away. A carefree person with nothing to do finds peace and happiness wherever they are.
Singing at the Sand-Pile Hermitage: "A single grain of sand contains worlds; boundless lands are not considered large. A child’s play builds a Buddha stupa."

As this mountain monk circumambulates, I forget all weariness and indolence. Why? Because this hermitage is free from entanglements and coverings. Towers, pavilions, halls, and chambers are without obstruction;
the kitchen hearth and the three gates are renewed day by day. Flocks of swallows fly back and forth as guests; yet who is the master within this hermitage remains unknown.
The Master of Masters has neither distance nor intimacy; he has no one to employ. Do not seek to scrutinize this further.

Treatise: Unmoved by the eight winds, all signs of flux have ceased. The ocean of awakening is perfectly luminous; the moon of the mind is serene and clear. Its essence is like a mirror, its function like a spirit:
when a barbarian comes, a Han appears, leaving no trace. The city walls and marketplaces are the Tathāgatagarbha;

within the body with form lies the formless body. Though the house is small, it is spacious and wide; the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and all sentient beings dwell therein. Birth, abiding, decay, and emptiness are but illusions.

Arising and ceasing; the foundation is firm and solid, as it has been from the beginning. Beneath the three rafters and within the six windows, eating and dressing require no preference for direction.
Throughout the vastness of past and present, all you heroic men—buying neighbors by the millions is but empty toil.
The title of this sutra is "Thus"—this is just so.
When the whirlwind topples the mountains, where could the ten directions and the three periods of time find even a hair’s breadth of a corner?
In spring the flowers bloom profusely; in autumn the wind falls the leaves. Do not disturb it in the least; it is naturally, vividly, and brilliantly present.
An Imitation of the Ancients: Composed for Lu Xiaonü of Pinghu Behold that Wuh Lake, pure and serene.
There dwelt a daughter of the Lu clan, known for her filial piety and integrity. (Stanza One) Without a father, whom could she rely upon? Her mother was compassionate;
she caressed and nurtured me, constant and affectionate from dawn until dusk. (Stanza Two) She saw to it that when I reached the age of maturity, she [prepared me] for marriage.

(Verse 3) She entered into marriage, yet her beauty remained unfulfilled; like a solitary wild goose, she sank into obscurity. (Verse 4) She vowed never to remarry, wishing only to care for her mother until the end.

She cut clouds and spun moonlight to weave her garments, never shrinking from toil or service. When her mother passed away and she alone remained, her tears flowed incessantly; in the end, she followed her mother in death.

She fulfilled both integrity and filial piety. (Verse 5) With a luminous mind and a single resolve, she saw her purpose through to the end; her spirit is now far-reaching, and her name remains in Eastern Zhejiang. (Verse 6)

Fourty-eight Verses on the Recitation of the Buddha’s Name One phrase of Amitābha accords with the nature; The nine grades of lotus flowers encompass the three vehicles. A single thought-moment of non-arising transcends provisional teachings;
One may ascend the golden terrace as a successor to the Buddha.

A single phrase of Amitābha levels the three periods of time; may the vow to propagate the six and eight [practices] be fulfilled in a single moment. Through the perfect cultivation and realization of the myriad practices over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one suddenly awakens to non-arising, wherein there is nothing that does not arise.
The wondrous realization of the single phrase "Amitābha" abides; in the emptiness of nature, both sin and merit leave no trace. Lotus flowers manifest according to one's mind;
always rely on the World-Honored One to hear the Dharma.
The principle of the Single Syllable Amitābha is spontaneously perfected; there is nothing to cultivate, nothing to realize, and no arising.
The Dharma King naturally possesses a realm of luminosity, walking step by step upon the ground of lapis lazuli.
A single phrase of Amitābha’s name—faith and vow are true. East and West lands do not depart from the person here and now. Within this, the three thousandfold world-realm is perfectly encompassed;
tree after tree, flower after flower, blooms in the same spring.

A single phrase of Amitābha is a lamp illuminating the world; it is capable of upholding the entire ocean of boundless teachings. Its originally wondrous truth penetrates both the ultimate and the conventional;
not lingering in mere Madhyamaka, it is the Supreme Vehicle.
Recite the name of Amitābha with single-minded resolve; what else can one seek that is higher?

With every sound filling the entire realm of empty space, all entanglements fall away like vines from a tree. (The Emperor Sejong of our dynasty said: "Simply take these four characters, 'A-mi-t'o-fo,' as the object of meditation;
in a single thought, they will last for ten thousand years, and you will naturally grasp your own nostrils.")
The single phrase of Amitābha takes the fruit as the cause; the natural father and son share the same essence. Grandly revealed is the face born of one’s mother;
take a confident step back home and do not turn your back on your kin.
The essence and function of the single phrase "Amitābha" are true; facing the sun, the entire body is revealed. In the realm beyond yin and yang, one performs somersaults;
in every land and every atom, the Dharma wheel turns.

A single phrase of Amitābha is recited from the mouth; yet the moment a thought arises, a thousand layers of separation intervene. How could one’s original reality wait for the light of reflection to illuminate it?
Infinite sounds are themselves the Dharma-lamp.
A single phrase of Amitābha purifies one's thoughts; when one is present, one is already born within the precious lotus. Why need one distinguish between the clarity and turbidity of the two lands?
Each and every person walks upon the crown of Vairocana’s head.
A single phrase of Amitābha accords with one’s own mind; the mark of the broad and long tongue is the true knower. The Buddhas of the six directions praise Amitābha Buddha in unison;
this is not merely the study of recitation and chanting.
With a single phrase of Amitābha, one delivers this life; one’s name is soon inscribed within the Land of Lotus Flowers.
The water of eight virtues is ever full, and the king of wish-fulfilling jewels naturally purifies the bones.

A single phrase of Amitābha turns the wheel of Dharma; where the conditional cause is thoroughly realized, the causal cause of enlightenment is true. Guarding the bright pearl with care, the root of precepts is pure;
in a single kṣaṇa, one realizes the fundamental cause.
A single phrase of Amitābha Buddha purifies the pulse; revealing the provisional to manifest the ultimate, one awakens to non-arising.
With perfect luminosity everywhere, this is the long-abiding path—what need is there to welcome the three carts outside the gate?

A single phrase of Amitābha dispels the miasma of evil; one suddenly transcends the multitude in the sea of suffering of Saṃsāra. The sound of the wind and the songs of birds discourse upon the True Dharma;
what does it matter whether the pure and the defiled are distinguished or not?

The single phrase of Amitābha is wondrously and uniquely supreme; there is no need to debate the interplay between nature and cultivation. Simultaneously obstructing and illuminating, body and mind are thoroughly penetrated;
the mutual integration of the primary and secondary realms is the gate of non-duality.
The single phrase "Amitābha" is the definitive cause; the path to the Land of Bliss has no place for lost travelers. Why seek further methods for settling the mind?
From the beginning, the fundamental suchness is the child returning to its parent.
Listen silently to the single phrase of Amitābha; with every sound, awaken the person of original nature.
As the hundred-and-eight bright pearls revolve in succession, countless auspicious rays of light issue from beneath the tongue.
The Samādhi of the Single Phrase Amitābha is accomplished; In secret communion with the sacred realm, the Buddha comes to welcome one.
The exquisite nature and characteristics of the Lotus Land— Without moving body or mind, one awakens to the clarity of the Dharma.
A single phrase of Amitābha is fundamentally most pure; the threefold cultivation perfectly embodies the cause within the fruit.
Now, do not inquire after the truth of suchness—this is the body beyond the body, entirely free of dependence.
Recite the name of Amitābha without ceasing; within the midst of worldly splendor, the dream has finally awakened. As the clouds part and the moon appears, its radiance fills all;
the flower-pavilion pervades the realm, and the ancient land is at peace.
A single phrase of Amitābha’s wondrous turning of the wheel— The Buddhas of the sands of the Ganges praise such a person. In resonance with their voices, the golden platform appears;
Sudden realization of non-arising is itself the Dharmakāya.
The definitive meaning of Amitābha is accomplished in a single phrase: with a straightforward mind, right mindfulness, and dedicated resolve;
through sincerity, without relying on artificial effort, it is achieved, and the layered flower-pavilions follow one’s own practice.

A single phrase of Amitābha possesses a distinct spiritual power; amidst the shadows of the red dust, the white lotus is fragrant. That the pond is deep and the flowers vast is but a secondary matter;
sitting in the dew upon the golden terrace, how tranquil is the dharma-realm!
A single phrase of Amitābha serves as the entrance for the spirit; mountains, rivers, and the great earth are utterly free of even a speck of dust. Adornments beyond measure manifest from the mind;
when the ground of the heart is tranquil, every season is spring.
A single phrase of Amitābha saves one from death and birth; The transcendent practices and vows are accomplished in an instant. From this point on, saṃsāra is suddenly stilled;
Coming and going are unobstructed, and the Dharma-realm is pure.
A single phrase of Amitābha washes away the dust from the mundane breast; few know the way beyond the Dharmakāya.
The majestic, true Buddha of daily life—refusing to turn one’s head, where else shall one seek?
The single phrase of Amitābha is a most wondrous gate; relying upon these four characters, one emerges from the cosmos.
This Dharma King’s supreme gāthā-medicine can only be taken by swallowing it whole in a single mouthful.
A single phrase of Amitābha resonates with stillness; boundless supreme companions have already arrived. When the original light is once emitted, drifting clouds disperse;
to see the Buddha is originally to see one’s own mind.
With a single phrase of Amitābha, the joy of the Dharma is perfected; the vast ocean of suffering is drained all at once.
Within crystal pavilions and lotus thrones, wisdom shines forth, illuminating the myriad dharmas in their manifold layers.
A single phrase of Amitābha purifies ten thousand thoughts; with the adamantine power of firm resolve, one sustains the body. Upon attaining birth in that land, one gains infinite life;
when the flowers bloom beneath the Bodhi tree, there is a spring all of its own.
A single phrase of Amitābha—every dharma is level; The six faculties are unimpeded, and the six sense-objects are pure. Primordially, the four lands have no high or low;
The fertile field of merit and wisdom requires no plowing.
A single phrase of Amitābha Buddha is wisdom and clarity; the pure land of the sole mind is neither born nor arising. From the beginning, body and land have never been separate;
lord and retinue are perfectly interfused in the level ocean of nature.
With the sincerity of a single phrase of Amitābha’s vow-power, one perfectly accomplishes ten recitations and departs for the West.
Even those of the lowest grade surely reach the shore, entrusting their essence to the lotus womb and escaping the four modes of birth.

Recite the single phrase of Amitābha with all one’s might; One will transcend the three miserable realms and eight difficulties. Holding his name extinguishes transgressions and the golden lotus appears;
His compassionate vows rely entirely upon the increase of the Buddha’s power.

A single phrase of Amitābha’s name brings the moon of wisdom; with the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness, the roots of goodness are deep. One directly ascends to the stage of non-retrogression and hastens toward An-yang (Sukhāvatī);
defilements, habitual tendencies, and worldly toil can no longer invade.
A single phrase of Amitābha is truly precious; the golden countenance of the Buddha appears within my own mind. In this life, I am ever weary of the sufferings of Saṃsāra;
I look afar toward the jeweled groves and lotus ponds.
With one phrase of Amitābha, one sees the original truth; turning the light back upon oneself, one is liberated from the cycle of delusion.
May the waters of the Eight Virtues Pond wash away all the dust of this Sahā world.
A single phrase of Amitābha preserves the power of wisdom; the profound and wondrous Dharma resides within this gate. It forges ordinary beings and refines the sages like a golden lion;
its golden form is translucent as it repays the Buddha’s grace. (Huayan is Sukhāvatī, Sukhāvatī is Huayan. A single phrase of Amitābha clears away worldly anxieties;
who that hears of the Pure Land would not seek rebirth there? It is only because that land is so magnificent and new.
The fruit: Cultivate the field of the mind with diligence;

the single phrase "Namu Amida Butsu" is beyond past and present. As the clouds of compassion gather thickly, my heart is redoubled in reverence. One should contemplate the setting sun like a suspended drum;
celestial music fills the void, and the dharma-sounds are profound.
A single phrase of Amitābha turns the wheel of thought; The five faculties and five powers adorn the body wondrously.
From this, hundreds of thousands of samādhis are attained; All virtues are cultivated together as the cause of non-retrogression.

(It seems Yongming is before one’s eyes. A single phrase of Amitābha is not invaded by external things; In every atom and every realm, my own mind appears. Boundless celestial music, a gentle breeze...
The offering continues: Furthermore, the kalaviṅka bird utters wondrous sounds;

a single phrase of Amitābha gladdens one's nature and mind. Through profound merit, one leaves behind appearances and flows against the current; with both [subject and object] vanished and both [clarity and stillness] illumined, the mind is untainted.
Detached from both "being" and "non-being," the Dharma-nature is equanimous.

A single phrase of Amitābha is wondrous beyond discourse; within the realm of the *Avataṃsaka*, it is the cause of the Ten Mysterious Gates. When one shatters the limits of conceptual thought, one knows there is no obstruction;

in a single thought-moment, the supreme wheel of Dharma is opened in unison. (Lingfu said: "This is remarkably similar to [the poems on] 'Mirror Images' and 'Bell Sounds. A single phrase of Amitābha: the realm is pure.
The natures and characteristics of the three thousand worlds are all perfectly luminous. When one quarter of the land is purified, every quarter is purified.
Pure. With single-minded devotion, every thought is refined;

with one invocation of Amitābha, the moon of the mind appears. The merit of the final thought resides in the very first thought; in a single moment, the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are perfected as non-dual.
Thus, because the cause is profound, the fruit is naturally profound.
Prayer Before the Stūpa of King Aśoka’s Relics, Burning My Finger in Aspiration:
I take refuge in the Great Vow-King, The stainless and pure radiance, The ocean of liberation and samādhi, Which washes away my mind and brings it cool relief.
Disciples such as I, together with all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, from beginningless time until now, have possessed two kinds of ignorance, which serve as the root of the two deaths.
We have been deluded regarding the truth and pursued the false; we have turned our backs on awakening and conformed to the dust of sensory objects.

Relying upon the three karmas and created by the six sense organs, the causes of evil—such as the five heinous crimes and the ten grave offenses—have become vast and extensive, resulting in endless fruits of suffering. We are submerged in the three miserable realms and buried deep within them.

Within the six realms of existence, due to causes, conditions, and past habitual tendencies, she was reborn as a woman. Though she studied the orthodox teachings without end, she failed to achieve success in cultivating pure karma.

Although she was included among the ranks of the Sangha, she had transgressed the precepts; subsequently, reflecting upon this with shame and remorse, she self-reproached herself and reverently burned off one finger as an offering to the precious stupa of the true-body relics of the Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, the Truth of Equality.

As with the Three Jewels of the One Essence, within the Lotus World, Amitābha Tathāgata, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the ocean-like assembly of Bodhisattvas all descend to bear witness, bestowing their empowerment and protection.

(As in the *De*) By provisionally employing illusory flames and the tip of a finger to smelt and refine the adamantine nature of wisdom, the radiance of insight blazes forth, tearing asunder the net of false views;
through wondrous contemplation and perfect penetration, the heavy veils of ignorance are shattered.

Within this realm, may all transgressions be extinguished; may one swiftly awaken to the Perfect and Sudden Supreme Vehicle, such that cultivation and realization are unified, and one enters directly into the nature-ocean of Vairocana.
Forgetting both body and mind, benefiting oneself and others within the light of equality, one shall certainly attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss.
The true realm of quiescent light will not be separated by even a hair’s breadth. Furthermore, I pray that at the time of death, the three minds shall be perfected.
The three obstacles are instantly eliminated; the lotus of the highest grade blossoms. The Buddha bestows the prophecy of Bodhi.
One serves the Buddhas of the ten directions and delivers all sentient beings, without weariness, until the end of the future.
Regarding "the present pivot" (*ji-ba-fu*):

since the time of the various ancient masters of old, after their own realization, whether seeing forms or hearing sounds, taking steps or swinging their arms, speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, blinking or raising an eyebrow—there was nothing that did not manifest the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). They...吐 (uttered).
This reveals the fundamental家风 (family style) of our school; it is what is called the "mechanism before one’s eyes.

Nevertheless, although both the sages of old and their later disciples have awakened to the original nature—which is neither one nor many—they remain unable to forget their intellectual views and are still captivated by the various conditions and circumstances before them.

Therefore, there are varying depths of awakening and differing degrees of pervasive perfection in vision. For the time being, among the various capacities before one, this Dharma-gate is the most extensive;
its meaning is exceedingly profound. Those who are deluded, at the gates of their six sense organs, pursue forms and follow sounds, racing outward in search of them without ever returning.

Those who awaken, upon encountering objects, turn back from conditions; they reverse the flow and revolve toward the One, dissolving away in that very place and attaining liberation wherever they are.
As for the transformation of function: it transforms the myriad things so that they dissolve back into oneself.
This is truly what opens the eye of wisdom for later students, thereby continuing the orthodox lineage of the predecessors.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, the assembly is addressed by comparing the Buddha to a "lion among men. Among the fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), there is only one bhikṣuṇī who bears the name "Lion.
This indicates that her majestic power was preeminent and that she had perfected the Buddha-mind; she was not [limited] by being a bhikṣuṇī.
Consequently, they have become weak. We have fallen into the ranks of the Sangha; we have altered our appearance and severed our attachments, leaving our kin and departing from our villages—what for?

Truly, it is because the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence is swift. It is merely to attain clear realization through a single phrase and to sever the cycle of samsara and its evil realms.
If it were for the sake of fame, profit, glory, or personal pleasure, it would not be the fundamental aspiration of one who has left the home life.

Alas! Those who have left the household life today, as soon as they have undergone tonsure, immediately become arrogant and deluded; failing to understand their own minds, they accept the prostrations and respect of others.
With such conduct, it is difficult for them to repay the four debts of gratitude. They have entered the Gate of Emptiness in vain—upon what can they rely?
Moreover, a human body is difficult to obtain and the Buddha-dharma is difficult to hear; having already obtained it and heard it, they yet fail to grasp it. Beneath the *kāṣāya* robe...

To clarify this matter, the suffering is truly boundless. Moreover, today the great community of bhikṣus still possesses the regulations for the meditation halls in the monasteries of various regions;
when the abbot provides instruction to permeate their hearing, although they may still be mired in delusion, they gradually attain clarity and penetration.
"We bhikṣuṇīs have none of this at all. All day long we are noisy, chasing after forms and following after sounds, rushing outward in our quest without ever reflecting inward.
As teachers, we do not instruct; as disciples, we do not learn. Time is to be cherished; a single life passes in an instant.
Though we have repeatedly returned to the human realm, we have gained nothing of benefit. Now, when a woman leaves the household life, she ought to cast aside the nature of a woman—"
Through practice, one plants the seeds of supreme excellence; by honoring eminent monks, one enters the Buddha-dharma with vigor.

With a mind of repentance and mindfulness of the Cool (Nirvana), one deeply arouses the heart of great compassion and fully carries out the deeds of liberation; only then does one become a model for the ten directions, causing the fourfold assembly to gather around in admiration.
I humbly hope that all you worthy ones will establish your resolve early on. Before your own fundamental matter is clarified, do not attend to other matters;
concentrate your mind on this single point and do not rest until it is fully realized. Now, this one matter is inherently possessed by every person and is already manifest in each and every one.

Yet, the source of the mind remains unexpanded and one drifts about chasing after external objects; this is truly because, throughout the day, one makes a living within the shadows of deluded thoughts. Do not...

One attains the ground of true realization. Whether practicing mindfulness of the Buddha or investigating through Zen meditation, one must, in all cases, gradually uproot the habitual tendencies and seeds of attachment accumulated throughout kalpas until they are completely shattered at once; only then will there be a place to begin.

Throughout the day, while engaged in a single practice, if habitual tendencies arise, sever them yourself and return to that single practice. When the power of this single practice becomes profound, even in stillness...
Within the subtle, one clearly perceives the seeds; one then eliminates them by means of a single practice. This single practice possesses power, and the seeds of craving wither of their own accord.
This is the eternal severance of the mental burdens of sentient beings. However, this single practice concerns neither Chan nor Pure Land; it is simply a state of solitary, vivid clarity.

If, throughout the twelve hours of the day, there is not a single thing [to distract you], yet throughout the twelve hours of the day, it seems as though there is always something [to attend to], only then is this true cultivation.
Furthermore, one must by no means allow even a single thought to involve itself with fame or gain.
As it is said, the divine nun did not manifest supernatural powers or preach the Dharma; rather, she simply practiced the two schools of Chan and Pure Land.

Whether one cultivates a single practice alone or practices both together, each person should follow their own capacity and skill, drawing near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and contemplating the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*) regarding all phenomena.
Mind and mind are equal. For one who applies effort in this manner, gaining power while reducing exertion, and reducing exertion while gaining power, such a person is a "divine nun" (shenní).
Why is this? Because they apply themselves directly and have never deceived themselves. When a lion attacks a tiger, it uses its full strength;
when a lion attacks a rabbit, it uses its full strength. Someone asked, "What kind of strength does it use? An ancient said: "None."
It is the power of deception. If one can indeed be free from deception, then throughout the twelve periods of the day, the fundamental radiance will abide eternally;

by diligently practicing a single path, one’s original nature will be suddenly revealed. At the assembly on Vulture Peak, six thousand bhikṣuṇīs had not yet received the prediction of their future Buddhahood.
Once the Dragon Girl emerged, the entire assembly was uplifted; thus, six thousand bhikṣuṇīs, though initially near the rank of Dharma masters, ultimately attained the stage of Buddhahood.

Yet, with a single yawn from the Lion’s Den, they had already perfected the fifty-three stages. If the bhikṣuṇīs were not themselves weak, then within the Dharmadhātu there would be no such thing as distance or proximity.
Why do you not reflect deeply upon this? At the time of your renunciation, what bitter and sweet experiences did you undergo?
Rush toward the Great Dharma. Study the lion’s stretch and completely cast off all the realms of women.
Restraining the body with pure regulations, the divine spirit will naturally distance itself from defilement. Do not settle for mediocrity; such are my true kinsmen.
